paragraphs.heading: Life at the scale of molecules
paragraphs.text: Molecular biology tries to explain living things by looking at the molecules inside and between cells and the chemistry they carry out. Most of its attention goes to nucleic acids, such as DNA and RNA, and to proteins. It asks how these big molecules are built, what they do and how they act on one another as a cell copies its DNA, reads its genes and makes proteins. The field borrows from genetics, biochemistry, physics, mathematics and, more lately, computer science, in a branch called bioinformatics.

paragraphs.heading: Why it arrived late
paragraphs.text: Cells and other tiny structures had been spotted in living things as early as the 18th century. Yet a detailed picture of how cells work only came in the 20th century, once tools from physics and chemistry were good enough to turn on living things. Molecular biology grew up where biochemistry and genetics meet, as both fields came to seek the molecular workings behind a cell's vital tasks. Its progress has gone hand in hand with new technologies and their refinement.

paragraphs.heading: From pea plants to DNA
paragraphs.text: Genetics began as an effort to understand heredity and the units of inheritance called genes. Gregor Mendel led the way in 1866, describing laws of inheritance from his crosses of pea plants. In 1869 the Swiss biochemist Friedrich Miescher studied pus-soaked bandages and found a phosphorus-rich substance he called nuclein, which we now know as DNA. In 1950 Erwin Chargaff showed that the order of DNA's building blocks differs between species, and that the purines always match the pyrimidines in total amount.

paragraphs.heading: The double helix and the code
paragraphs.text: In 1953 James Watson and Francis Crick published DNA's double helix, drawing on X-ray crystallography by Rosalind Franklin that reached them through Maurice Wilkins and Max Perutz. They also guessed at what the shape might mean for how DNA is copied. Watson, Crick and Wilkins shared the 1962 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. In 1961 it was shown that a gene spells out a protein three DNA letters at a time, each triplet, or codon, standing for one amino acid, read from a fixed start without overlaps.

paragraphs.heading: Proving genes are DNA
paragraphs.text: In 1928 Frederick Griffith worked with pneumococcus bacteria that were killing lab rats. One strain was smooth and deadly, coated in a polysaccharide capsule that hid it from the host's immune system; the other was rough, lacked the capsule and was easily destroyed. Griffith proposed that genes could pass between members of the same generation, now called genetic transformation. Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase confirmed that DNA is the genetic material: working with E. coli and a bacteriophage, they tagged the phage's protein coat and its DNA with different radioactive labels, and found that the DNA a phage injects into a bacterium holds everything needed to build new phages.

paragraphs.heading: Why it matters today
paragraphs.text: Molecular biology gives scientists techniques for studying the processes inside cells. Those methods help aim new drugs, diagnose disease and understand how cells function. Some treatments that grew out of the field fall under gene therapy, and its use in medicine is now known as molecular medicine.
